strengths: The focus on social activities addresses a meaningful gap in object-centric cultural evaluation. CULTIVate provides substantial coverage: 576 prompts, 16 countries, nine activity categories, and six image generators.

The descriptor-based framework provides interpretable diagnostics across objects, attire, background, interactions, and spatial arrangements, making its assessments more inspectable than a single image–text similarity score.

Table 2 provides encouraging evidence: FAITH achieves Spearman correlation of 0.38 with human judgments, compared with 0.22 for VQAScore and 0.33 for ALIGN alone. Recruitment based on nationality and residence, annotation quality controls, and proposer–refiner ablations are positive aspects.
weaknesses: The central metrics have unresolved validity problems. ALIGN rewards coverage of descriptors that explicitly include optional and mutually exclusive variants, potentially penalizing a fully valid individual scene. HAL treats any unmatched descriptor as incorrect, although absence from a finite reference list does not establish cultural inappropriateness. The reported 90.27% descriptor relevance validates neither reference completeness nor image-descriptor extraction accuracy.

DDIV measures entropy across descriptor frequencies rather than variation between images. Repeating the same image containing several descriptors can therefore yield high diversity, even maximal diversity if all reference descriptors are present equally often. Neither diversity metric receives human validation or controlled tests establishing the intended behavior.

EXAG relies on only five Google-search references per prompt, selected using CLIPScore—the kind of alignment metric the paper criticizes for rewarding stereotypes. These references are not established as representative or free of exaggeration. Consequently, deviation from their mean similarity may reflect reference selection or legitimate cultural variation rather than exaggeration. The paper also does not adequately specify the alignment function used in this metric.

Human validation is insufficiently documented and statistically supported. The study covers seven countries and three public generators, but does not clearly report participant counts, ratings per image, or how human–human agreement is calculated. Correlations lack confidence intervals or significance tests, and a separate held-out set for validating threshold and metric choices is not established. Generalization to the remaining countries and proprietary models is therefore uncertain.

Several claims exceed the reported evidence. Table 7 gives EXAG an overall correlation of 0.26 with human exaggeration ratings, below QwenVL's 0.29, despite claims of superior performance. HAL's overall advantage over QwenVL is only 0.30 versus 0.29. The headline '7% better correlation' is not transparently reconciled with Table 2, and VQAScore's 0.22 correlation contradicts the blanket description of alignment methods as having approximately zero agreement.

The Global North–South comparisons do not isolate cultural representation disparities from differences in activity composition, prompt difficulty, reference coverage, or evaluator bias. Country-specific activity sets and LLM-generated references can introduce systematic measurement differences. Group means without uncertainty, matched comparisons, or broader human confirmation do not adequately support the strongest claims of consistent bias across countries.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the descriptor extractor is inconsistently identified as InternVL2.5 and InternVL3-14B, several appendix prompts visibly extend beyond page boundaries, and important generation and evaluation settings are missing. Although the benchmark direction is promising, the unresolved measurement issues and limited validation leave the contribution below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The focus on culturally situated social activities is useful and well motivated. Evaluating interactions and contextual variants complements existing object-centric cultural benchmarks.
CULTIVate offers substantial coverage: 576 prompts across 16 countries and nine activity categories, with over 19,000 generated images from six models and approximately 3,000 reference images.

The descriptor framework provides interpretable diagnostics. Table 2 reports a meaningful improvement in human faithfulness correlation: 0.38 for FAITH versus 0.22 for the strongest listed baseline, VQAScore.
The paper includes local participant recruitment, descriptor validation averaging 90.27% relevance, and ablations supporting the proposer–refiner pipeline.
weaknesses: The central metrics do not adequately distinguish cultural faithfulness from reference coverage. ALIGN rewards covering descriptors that can be optional or mutually exclusive, including when evaluating individual images. HAL treats every unmatched descriptor as erroneous, although a finite reference list cannot exhaust valid cultural variation. Descriptor relevance validation establishes neither completeness nor reliable identification of genuinely incorrect elements.

The pipeline’s dependence on model-generated cultural knowledge remains insufficiently validated. LLMs generate the references and an MLLM extracts image descriptors, so evaluator bias can contribute to the reported geographical disparities. The supplied detector prompts compound this concern: Table 22 instructs the detector to 'Always include both traditional and modern possibilities,' which can encourage plausible descriptions rather than strictly observed content. No extraction-accuracy audit or evaluator-backbone robustness study establishes that these effects are controlled.

EXAG has unresolved validity and reproducibility issues. It compares an image’s maximum stereotype similarity against averages from only five search-selected references per prompt, without establishing that this measures exaggeration rather than legitimate scene variation. CLIPScore-based reference selection may introduce the same stereotypical preferences criticized elsewhere. The scoring function f, stereotype-generation procedure, and compatibility of EXAG’s scale with the arithmetic FAITH aggregate are insufficiently specified.

Human validation is limited relative to the claims: 189 generated-image evaluation forms cover seven countries and three public models, excluding all proprietary generators. Participant counts, ratings per image, aggregation procedures, and the calculation of human–human agreement are insufficiently documented. No confidence intervals or significance tests establish the reliability of metric improvements, and a clearly independent validation split for threshold selection is not described.

The diversity contribution is not adequately established. Descriptor entropy can be maximal when every generated image contains the same complete descriptor set, despite there being no variation between images. The paper explicitly provides no human validation of diversity and does not compare against established diversity measures. Moreover, Table 1 shows higher SDIV for Global South countries in two of three public models, contradicting the accompanying claim of consistently lower diversity.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Country-group averages do not establish consistently worse performance in every country, and country-specific activity difficulty and evaluator accuracy are not disentangled from generator bias. Appendix A.5 claims the highest exaggeration correlation, but Table 7 gives EXAG 0.26 versus QwenVL’s 0.29. Reproducibility is also weakened by conflicting extractor identifiers and visibly clipped appendix prompts. Overall, the benchmark is promising, but unresolved measurement and validation problems place the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The focus on culturally situated social activities is meaningful: interactions and contextual variations expose failures that object-centric benchmarks can miss.
CULTIVate provides substantial experimental breadth, covering 576 prompts, 16 countries, nine activity categories, and six recent image generators, with approximately 3,000 real reference images.
Descriptor-based evaluation offers interpretable diagnostics across attire, objects, background, interactions, and spatial arrangement.

Human evaluation provides encouraging evidence: FAITH achieves Spearman correlation 0.38 versus 0.22 for the strongest reported baseline, VQAScore. Descriptor relevance averages 90.27%, and the proposer–refiner ablation improves alignment correlation.
weaknesses: The core metrics conflate descriptor coverage with cultural correctness. ALIGN rewards coverage of descriptors explicitly allowed to be optional or mutually exclusive, potentially penalizing a valid individual scene. HAL treats every unmatched descriptor as incorrect, although finite reference lists cannot enumerate all legitimate cultural variants. The descriptor relevance study measures precision, not the completeness needed to justify this closed-world assumption.

The evaluation does not establish that the pipeline avoids inherited cultural bias. Reference descriptors come from LLMs, and image descriptors come from an MLLM whose prompts request typical scenes and both traditional and modern possibilities rather than strictly observed content. There is no direct validation of image-descriptor extraction accuracy or robustness across extractors. These issues undermine attribution of measured errors to the image generators.

EXAG relies on only five search images per prompt, selected using CLIPScore—the same family of alignment methods criticized for rewarding stereotypes. Their representativeness is not established. Departures from average reference similarity can reflect legitimate variation rather than exaggeration. Moreover, Table 7 reports lower overall exaggeration correlation for EXAG than QwenVL, 0.26 versus 0.29, contradicting the accompanying superiority claim.

Human validation is limited to 189 generated-image forms across seven countries and three public models. The number of annotators, ratings per image, aggregation procedure, and human–human correlation calculation are insufficiently specified. No confidence intervals or significance tests are supplied, and no clearly held-out protocol establishes generalization after threshold selection. This makes the reliability of metric improvements difficult to assess.

Descriptor diversity has a concrete validity problem: identical images containing every reference descriptor yield maximum DDIV despite having no between-image diversity. Diversity receives no human validation. Similarly, country-group comparisons lack controls for differences in activity difficulty and reference quality; they establish score disparities on this benchmark more convincingly than broad cultural-bias conclusions.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. The implementation inconsistently names InternVL2.5 and InternVL3-14B, leaves the EXAG scoring function and stereotype-candidate generation insufficiently specified, and provides visibly clipped prompts. No code or dataset release location is supplied. Several claims also conflict with tables: GS semantic diversity is not consistently lower, and Table 10's reported average does not match its listed values. Overall, the promising benchmark is not yet supported by sufficiently reliable measurement and validation for acceptance.

strengths: CULTIVate targets a meaningful gap: cultural representation through social activities, interactions, and spatial arrangements rather than primarily isolated artifacts. Coverage of 576 activities across 16 countries and six generators constitutes a substantial evaluation effort.
The descriptor-based framework provides interpretable diagnostics, with a useful distinction between cultural coverage, unsupported elements, exaggeration, and diversity.

Human evaluation provides concrete evidence of improvement over image–text similarity metrics and matched-backbone judges. In Table 2, FAITH reaches Spearman correlations of 0.42 and 0.47, versus 0.10 and 0.20 for the corresponding direct judges.

The paper includes nationality-matched annotators, descriptor validation, two evaluation backbones, component ablations, and extensive implementation prompts. These are valuable steps toward assessing reliability and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core metrics conflate valid cultural variation with error. ALIGN measures coverage of a reference set explicitly containing mutually exclusive variants, yet the principal faithfulness evaluation uses individual images. A faithful image showing one valid variant can therefore receive lower alignment than an implausible image combining alternatives. Similarly, HAL treats every unmatched descriptor as incorrect, although a finite reference set cannot exhaust legitimate scenes. Reported descriptor precision and subjective coverage ratings do not establish the completeness required by this interpretation.

The actual image-extraction prompts undermine the claim that MLLMs perform only generic visual parsing. Tables 22–25 ask for culturally typical scenes, common variations, and explicitly instruct the attire extractor to 'Always include both traditional and modern possibilities.' These instructions can elicit expected content absent from the image. No independently annotated extraction evaluation establishes that scores measure depicted content rather than the extractor's cultural priors.

EXAG has an insufficiently validated reference distribution. It compares each generated image against only five web images selected using CLIPScore, despite the paper's evidence that CLIPScore is unreliable for cultural faithfulness. Positive deviation from average similarity does not by itself establish exaggeration: a legitimate cultural variant can exceed that average. Sensitivity to reference selection and controlled tests separating authentic cultural cues from exaggerated ones are missing. Table 9 also shows that the adopted ITA-based EXAG correlates less well with human exaggeration judgments than the Qwen direct judge.

The headline superiority claim is overstated. Table 2 reports 0.47 for the strongest FAITH configuration versus 0.48 for GPT-4o judging. The advertised '27% higher correlation' is an absolute increase of 0.27 over the weaker InternVL3 judge, not an improvement over the strongest baseline. Since AHEaD receives external knowledge generated by GPT-4o and Gemini, a judge supplied with the same reference descriptors is also needed to isolate the benefit of the proposed scoring mechanism.

The evidence does not establish that all three faithfulness components are necessary. Table 3 improves overall correlation from 0.41 to 0.47 for InternVL3 and from 0.39 to 0.42 for Qwen; adding HAL alone leaves Qwen's overall correlation unchanged and lowers its GS correlation. Reported significance of correlations does not establish significance of differences between dependent correlations. Confidence intervals, paired comparisons, and a clearly separated validation/test protocol are needed, particularly because threshold choice is justified using human-correlation results.

Human validation is limited relative to the breadth of the conclusions: it covers three public generators, two ratings per image, and country-level agreement ranging from 0.15 to 0.62. The proprietary-model evaluations lack corresponding human validation. Country-specific activity sets also confound cultural disparities with differences in activity difficulty; the observed GN–GS gaps warrant more qualified interpretation and matched-activity analysis.

Several reporting gaps impede verification. Tables 4–5 do not clearly reconcile their correlation values with the main ALIGN results, and Table 10's reported average of 0.183 does not match its three displayed values. Table 11 validates GPT-4o descriptors rather than clearly documenting validation of the final proposer–refiner references. Diversity metrics receive little independent validation, and image refinement is supported only by four qualitative examples.

strengths: CULTIVate addresses a meaningful gap by evaluating culturally situated social activities, including interactions and spatial arrangements, rather than primarily isolated objects. Its 576 activities, 16 countries, and six generators provide useful breadth.

The descriptor-based framework offers interpretable diagnostics for missing, unsupported, and exaggerated elements. Separating these dimensions is potentially valuable for understanding generation failures.

Table 2 provides concrete evidence of improvement over matched-backbone judges: Spearman correlation increases from 0.20 to 0.47 for InternVL3 and from 0.10 to 0.42 for Qwen2.5-VL. Results across two backbones strengthen this finding.
The paper includes human evaluation with nationality-matched participants, descriptor validation, component ablations, and detailed prompts and implementation settings.
weaknesses: The central metrics have unresolved construct-validity problems. ALIGN rewards coverage of reference descriptors that explicitly include mutually exclusive cultural variants, while the principal faithfulness results use individual images. A valid image need not contain every variant. HAL treats any unmatched descriptor as incorrect, conflating reference incompleteness with cultural hallucination. Approximately 90% descriptor precision and subjective coverage ratings do not establish the completeness required for this inference.

The claim that descriptor extraction avoids reliance on MLLM cultural biases is insufficiently supported. The extraction prompts explicitly request cultural expertise, typical scenes, and culturally specific terminology; the attire prompt even requests both traditional and modern possibilities. These instructions risk eliciting prior expectations rather than strictly observed content. There is no direct human validation of extracted descriptors or semantic matches to quantify this failure mode.

EXAG relies on only five web images per prompt, selected using CLIPScore, despite the paper demonstrating that CLIPScore can favor culturally incorrect or stereotypical imagery. A maximum positive deviation from this small reference mean can penalize legitimate variation and does not directly establish exaggeration. Reference-selection sensitivity and stronger validation are needed. Table 9 also shows that the chosen EXAG method correlates less well with human exaggeration judgments than the Qwen judge, 0.29 versus 0.34.

The headline superiority claim overstates the evidence. The reported '+27%' is an absolute correlation increase of 0.27 over the matched InternVL3 baseline, not a 27% relative improvement. FAITH's overall correlation of 0.47 does not exceed GPT-4o's 0.48. Since GPT-4o and Gemini also supply reference knowledge, a descriptor-informed judge baseline is needed to isolate the benefit of the proposed scoring mechanism from access to stronger models' cultural knowledge.

Statistical support for the necessity of the composite metric is inadequate. Table 3 improves correlation from 0.41 to 0.47 for InternVL3 and from 0.39 to 0.42 for Qwen; adding HAL alone does not improve Qwen's overall result. Reported significance of individual correlations does not establish significance of their differences. Paired confidence intervals or bootstrap tests are missing, and an explicit held-out protocol for threshold selection is not described.

Human validation is limited relative to the benchmark's scope: 398 forms, two ratings per form, 11 countries, and three public generators. Krippendorff's alpha ranges from 0.15 to 0.62, with regional averages of 0.28 and 0.35, leaving substantial uncertainty. The paper does not establish metric reliability for proprietary generators or report sufficiently detailed country-level uncertainty to support broad generalization.

The Global North–South findings are suggestive but insufficiently disentangled from differences in activity difficulty, descriptor coverage, and evaluator bias. Countries have different activity inventories, and national labels obscure substantial internal cultural variation. Human averages support the direction of the aggregate gap, but matched-activity analyses and uncertainty estimates are needed before attributing it confidently to generator disparities.

strengths: The focus on culturally situated social activities is meaningful and extends evaluation beyond objects, clothing, and landmarks. CULTIVate offers substantial breadth: 576 activities across 16 countries, six generators, and over 19,000 generated images.

The descriptor-based framework provides interpretable diagnostics across objects, attire, interactions, backgrounds, and spatial arrangements. This is potentially useful for understanding failures and guiding image editing.

Table 2 provides convincing evidence of improvement over conventional image–text metrics and same-backbone judges: InternVL3-based FAITH reaches Spearman correlation 0.47, versus 0.20 for direct judging and 0.04 for CLIPScore.

The evaluation includes culturally matched human annotators, descriptor validation, two evaluator backbones, component ablations, and detailed prompts. These are valuable efforts toward validating an otherwise difficult evaluation task.
weaknesses: The central metrics have unresolved construct-validity problems. HAL treats any descriptor absent from a finite reference set as hallucinated, conflating legitimate unlisted variation with cultural error. ALIGN rewards coverage of alternative descriptors even when one image should depict only one valid variant. Approximately 90% reference precision and informal omission reports do not establish the completeness or contextual compatibility needed to justify these interpretations.

The claim that descriptor extraction avoids cultural biases is insufficiently supported. The extraction prompts explicitly invoke cultural expertise and typical scenes; Table 25 even requests both traditional and modern possibilities. These instructions could elicit expected rather than observed content. There is no direct human audit of extracted descriptors or controlled test separating extraction errors from generator errors.

EXAG depends on only five web images per prompt, selected using CLIPScore—the same family of metrics criticized for rewarding stereotypes. Appendix A.3 assumes real images contain no incorrect or exaggerated elements, which is not established. Without auditing references or testing alternative sampling procedures, the score may measure deviation from biased search results rather than exaggeration.

The headline superiority claim overstates the results. FAITH's 0.47 correlation does not exceed GPT-4o judging at 0.48; the reported '+27%' is an absolute 0.27 increase over the weaker InternVL3 baseline. Baselines supplied with the same reference descriptors are missing, so gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed metric rather than additional cultural information. Evaluation cost is also not compared.

Statistical support for the necessity of all components is inadequate. FAITH improves over ALIGN by only 0.03–0.06, and Table 3's significance of individual correlations does not establish significance of their differences. Confidence intervals, paired comparisons accounting for shared activities/countries, and a clearly held-out calibration protocol are needed. Human agreement is also limited: country-level alpha ranges from 0.15 to 0.62.

The Global North–South interpretation is not adequately separated from activity difficulty, reference quality, and evaluator bias. Countries have different activity inventories, while the paper itself finds large differences between universal and culturally specific activities. Matched comparisons and country-level uncertainty are needed before attributing aggregate gaps confidently to generator bias. These unresolved measurement and validation issues outweigh the benchmark's promise for acceptance.
